title: School-Bus-Sized Whale Sharks Spotted Off Florida — and They're Gentle Giants!
summary: Have you ever seen a fish as long as a school bus? That's the whale shark — the biggest fish in the world! And recently, scientists in Florida spotted some of these gentle giants swimming about eight miles west of Loggerhead Key in the Dry Tortugas. They used a special underwater camera called S-BRUV, which usually watches reef fish. But this time, it captured amazing footage of whale sharks gliding through the water. Whale sharks can grow up to 60 feet long — that's as long as a bowling lane or a fishing boat. Even their babies are born two feet long! They're filter feeders, which means they swim with their huge mouths open to scoop up tiny plankton, small fish, and crustaceans. Douglas Adams, a scientist with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, says they help keep the ocean's plankton in balance. And don't worry — they're completely harmless to humans. But these spotted sharks are endangered. They face dangers like getting caught in fishing nets, boat strikes, and climate change. That's why tracking them with cameras like S-BRUV is so important. If you're in Florida and see one, you can report it to help scientists protect them. Who knows? Maybe you'll be the next person to spot a real-life gentle giant!
why_it_matters: Whale sharks help keep the ocean healthy by controlling plankton. Learning to protect them means keeping our oceans balanced, and that affects all of us who eat seafood or enjoy beach trips.

background_read: Whale sharks are not whales; they are sharks, but they are harmless to humans because they eat only tiny sea creatures. They can be found in warm oceans around the world.
The Dry Tortugas is a group of small islands in the Gulf of Mexico, part of the Florida Keys, and it's a national park known for its clear waters and sea life.
Scientists use special cameras like S-BRUV to study fish without disturbing them. This helps them learn about where whale sharks travel and how to protect them.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, like Douglas Adams.
WHAT: They spotted and filmed whale sharks near Loggerhead Key using an S-BRUV camera.
WHERE: About eight miles west of Loggerhead Key in the Dry Tortugas, Florida.
WHY: To track and protect these endangered gentle giants from dangers like nets, boats, and climate change.

perspectives.description: Seeing these huge fish shows that conservation efforts can work if we protect their habitats. Whale sharks attract tourists and are important for ocean health.
But these creatures are still endangered because of human activities like overfishing and plastic pollution. More needs to be done to stop accidental catches and slow down boats.
Tracking them with cameras gives scientists data to understand their migration patterns and how climate change is warming their waters.
